texts.facts: It is the case of the complainant that the complainant, Muskan Container Lines Pvt. Ltd., registered under the Companies Act, 1956, operates from multiple offices across India and abroad, maintaining various port accounts. Manager, is the company's Authorised Representative for this case, as per a Board Resolution dated 09.12.2019. The complaint names Accused No.1 as a company, with Accused No.2, one of its directors, responsible for its day-to-day operations. In August 2019, Accused No.2 contacted the complainant's Mumbai office to arrange the export of 8 containers of rice. The complainant confirmed the shipment and issued a Bill of Lading (No. MCLPL/MUM/JEA/469/19) for the journey from Nhava Sheva, Mumbai, to Jebel Ali, Dubai. The shipper was Shri Siddhivinayak Import and Export Company from Pune, and the consignee was Soha Arif Foodstuff Trading, Ajman Free Zone, UAE. Accused No.1 was acting as the authorised customs broker for the shipper. After the complainant received payment of Rs.88,688 via cheque No. 500163 dated 19.08.2019, they issued the original Master Bill of Lading to Accused No.2. On 24.08.2019, Accused No.2 emailed the complainant, instructing them to hold delivery of 3 containers. On 26.08.2019, a similar instruction was provided by the shipper to the complainant's Belapur office. The shipper later informed the complainant that the consignee had taken delivery of 5 containers under Bill of Lading No. MCLPL/MUM/JEA/469/19 without an original delivery order, using fake documents and failing to make M/s Muskan Containers Line Pvt. Ltd. Vs. M / s All Bound Global Freight Pvt. Ltd. Digitally signed Page no. 3 / 34 by ARVIND ARVIND TOMAR TOMAR Date: 2024.11.28 16:38:52 +0600 payment. Dubai Customs requires an original delivery order for container release, and the shipper filed a complaint with Dubai authorities. The complainant's agent in Dubai confirmed that no delivery order had been issued from their office. On 24.10.2019, Accused No.2 and the shipper sent letters to the Muskan Container Lines Pvt. Accused No.2 also issued cheque No. 143336 dated 25.10.2019, drawn on IndusInd Bank, Navi Mumbai, for Rs.5,00,000 as a partial payment, with a promise to settle the remaining balance upon invoicing. The complainant, relying on the previous payment of Rs.88,688, presented the cheque on 05.11.2019 to its bank, AU Small Finance Bank, Dwarka, Delhi. However, on 06.11.2019, the cheque was dishonoured with the reason "Payment Stopped by Drawer." Despite efforts to contact Accused No.2, the complainant received no response. The complainant then served a legal notice on 20.11.2019, which was received by the accused on 22.11.2019 and 23.11.2019. As the payment remains outstanding, the complainant has filed a complaint under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, claiming jurisdiction in this court. M/s Muskan Containers Line Pvt. Ltd. Vs . M/s All Bound Global Freight Pvt. Ltd. 3. Prima facie case was found to be made out against the accused persons, cognizance of offence punishable u/s 138 of the NI Act was taken and they were summoned. Upon entering appearance, the substance of accusation was served to the accused persons through accused no.2 on 23.12.2022 wherein he pleaded not guilty but admitted issuing the cheque. He admitted that the cheque bears his signatures and that the amount was filled by him. He denied filling other particulars. The accused admitted the receipt of demand notice. He further stated that he is a custom broker and a consignment was sent to dubai by his client M/S Siddhi Vinayak and was delivered without original delivery order and consignee did not make the payment to the consignor so consignor stopped the container in dubai port as she observed documentational lapse and intentional fraud. To recover these charges the complainant in India held his other customer's import shipment and tried to pressurise him for the payment which was not his liability. The case was proceeded with and in support of the allegations made in the complaint, the complainant, adopted his pre-summoning evidence by way of affidavit Ex. CW1/A and relied upon the documents already exhibited at the time of pre-summoning evidence as follows: a. Ex. CW1/1: Copy of board resolution in favour of Mr. Rahul. Ex.CW1/11 to Ex.CW1/18: Postal receipts, courier receipts and proof of delivery. STATEMENT OF ACCUSED 5. Thereafter, statement u/s. 313 Cr.P.C. of the accused no.2 was recorded on behalf of the accused persons in which he stated that there was no liability to pay the complainant and that the cheque was forcefully collected by holding their other customer's shipment. As there was no liability, the company stopped payment. He stated that the company was already in communication through email with the complainant before the legal notice was received. He further stated that it was a complete mistake of the complainant company as containers under subject shipment were released to consignee without original delivery order by the complainant and containers were evacuated from port without submission of original documents due to which their client M/S Shree Siddhi Vinayak Company faced a huge loss and balance 3 containers were put on hold by them to investigate and that they have filed complaint in UAE for the same. It also came to their knowledge that the balance of 3 containers were auctioned and charges were recovered by the complainant. CC NI Act 44830/2019 ARVIND TOMAR M/s Muskan Containers Line Pvt. Ltd. Ld. predecessor had permitted the accused to file an affidavit in lieu of examination in chief (Ex. AW-A) wherein he stated that M/s All Bound Global Freight Pvt. Ltd. ("Accused No. 1") is a Custom House Agent that arranged an export of eight containers of rice to Jebel Ali port in Dubai for its client, M/s Shree Siddhivinayak Import And Export Company. The booking was made on 09/08/2019 through the Complainant shipping agent. Accused No. 1 completed all customs formalities, and the shipment was loaded and documented under Shipping Bill No. 6232097 dated 13/08/2019. 7. On 24/08/2019, Accused No. 1's client reported that five containers were released by an unauthorised party without payment, allegedly due to the Complainant's negligence in releasing the containers without the original delivery order. Dubai authorities confirmed that the containers were released based on fake documents. The Complainant placed a hold on further container releases at the request of Accused No. 1's client, resulting in ground rent charges at the port. Accused No. 1 contended these charges were not its responsibility but due to the Complainant's error. Despite this, the Complainant demanded payment of the ground rent and allegedly withheld other consignments booked by Accused No. 1, which led to the loss of Accused No. 1's client, M/s Hinjawadi Infra Development Pvt. Ltd. Under pressure, Accused No. 1 issued a cheque of 5,00,000, though it maintains there was no legal obligation for payment. 9. Accused persons have relied on the following documents (as referenced in the affidavit filed) to support their case: a. Ex.AW-1/1: Email from the Complainant regarding M/s Qamar Al Samha's letter. Ex. AW-1/4: Accused No. 1's email dated 31/10/2019 to the Complainant, outlining the dispute and denying any liability for charges. M/s All Bound Global Freight Pvt. Ltd. 10 . Lastly, Accused no.2 stated that the Complainant's actions are a result of malafide intentions to recover costs improperly, has filed the present complaint for payment that he contends is baseless, after which the defence evidence was closed and the case was put for final argument. Perusal of the facts of the case in light of the bare provision and the Krishna Janardhan Bhat judgment, reveal the following necessary ingredients of the offence. 15. First Ingredient: The cheque was drawn by the accused on an account maintained by him for payment of money to the drawer and the same is presented for payment within a period of 3 months from the date on which it is drawn or within the period of its validity; 15.1 With respect to this ingredient, the complainant has, in his complaint as well as his affidavit, alleged that the cheque in controversy was issued to him by the accused no.2 on behalf of accused no.1 on an account maintained by the accused no.1 at their bank. To prove the allegation, the complainant relied on the statements of the accused no.2, one recorded at the stage of issuing notice u/s 251 CrPC and u/s 313 CrPC where he has admitted his signatures, filling in the amount and issuing the cheque in question.

Counsel for the complainant argued that all essentials of the offence as enumerated in Ch. 17 of the NI act are made out beyond reasonable doubt against the accused and prayed that the accused be convicted, sentenced as per law. 12. Per contra, ld. Counsel for the accused has argued that there existed no legally enforceable debt/liability of the accused towards the complainant and that the complainant had pressured the accused to make payment as a condition to release the import shipment of the accused's customer. It was for the safety of his importer and business that the accused had issued the cheques as the complainant was not releasing the consignment. Ld. counsel also highlighted the infirmities in the testimony of the complainant and prayed that the Digitally 10 / 34 signed by ARVIND ARVIND TOMAR M/s Muskan Containers Line Pvt. Ltd. Vs. Ld. counsel for the accused placed reliance on Hon'ble Supreme court of India's judgment in case titled Sampelly Satynarayana Rao vs. Indian Renewable Energy development Agency limited ( AIR 2016 SUPREME COURT 4363) & M/S Indus Airways Pvt. Ltd And Ors vs M/S Magnum Aviation Pvt Ltd And Anr (AIR ONLINE 2014 SC 89). S. 138 of the NI acts reads as follows, "Where any cheque drawn by a person on an account maintained by him with a banker for payment of any amount of money to another person from out of that account for the discharge, in whole or in part, of any debt or other liability, is returned by the bank unpaid, either because of the amount of money standing to the credit of that account is insufficient to honour the cheque or that it exceeds the amount arranged to be paid from that account by an agreement made with that bank, such person shall be deemed to have committed an offence and shall without prejudice to any other provisions of this Act, be punished with imprisonment for a term which may extend to two year, or with fine which may extend to twice the amount of the cheque, or with both: Provided that nothing contained in this section shall apply unless- (a) The cheque has been presented to the bank within a period of six months from the date on which it is drawn or within the period of its validity, whichever is earlier. (b) The payee or the holder in due course of the cheque, as the case may be, makes a demand for the payment of the said amount of money by giving a notice, in writing, to the drawer, of the cheque, within thirty days of the receipt of information by him from the bank regarding the return of the cheques as unpaid, and (c) The drawer of such cheque fails to make the payment of the said amount of money to the payee or, as the case may be, to the holder in due course of the cheque, within fifteen days of the receipt of the said notice. Explanation: For the purpose of this section, "debt or other liability" means a legally enforceable debt or other liability. 16.1 S.146 of the NI act, 1881 states that " The Court shall, in respect of every proceeding under this Chapter, on production of bank's slip or memo having thereon the official mark denoting that the cheque has been dishonoured, presume the fact of dishonour of such cheque, unless and until such fact is disproved." 16.2 --Until the contrary is proved, the following presumptions shall be made: --(a) of consideration -- that every negotiable instrument was made or drawn for consideration, and that every such instrument, when it has been accepted, indorsed, negotiated or transferred, was accepted, indorsed, negotiated or transferred for consideration; S. 139: Presumption in favour of holder.-- It shall be presumed, unless the contrary is proved, that the holder of a cheque received the cheque of the nature referred to in section 138 for the discharge, in whole or in part, of any debt or other liability. 18.2 In Rangappa V. Sri Mohan (2010) 11 SCC 441, a three judge bench observed that, "Section 139 of the NI Act is stated to be an example of a reverse onus clause which is in tune with the legislative intent of improving the credibility of negotiable instruments. The offence under Section 138 of the NI Act is at best a regulatory offence and largely falls in the arena of a civil wrong and therefore the test of proportionality ought to guide the interpretation of the reverse onus clause. An accused may not be expected to discharge an unduly high standard of proof. The standard of Muskan Container Lines Pvt. Ltd vs M/S All Bound Global Freight Pvt. Ltd on 28 November, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/16703060/ 10 proof for doing so would necessarily be on the basis of "preponderance of probabilities" and not "beyond shadow of any doubt"." The Hon'ble Supreme Court in Dayabhai Chhaganbhai Thakkar vs State of Gujarat (1964) 7 SCR 361, held that: "Even if the accused fails to prove his defence to the extent of preponderance of probability but if it is sufficient enough to raise doubt on the story of complaint, it will be the complainant who will be said to have failed in discharging the guilt of the accused beyond reasonable doubt." In Parminder Kaur @ P.P. Kaur @ Soni vs State of Punjab [CrA 283 of 2011], the apex court has held that 18 / 34 Digitally signed by ARVIND CC NI Act 44830/2019 ARVIND TOMAR M/s Muskan Containers Line Pvt. Ltd. Vs. M/s All Bound Global Freight Pvt. Ltd. TOMAR Date: 2024.11.28 16:41:00 +0600 "Unlike the prosecution which needs to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt, the accused merely needs to create reasonable doubt or prove their alternate version by mere preponderance of probabilities." However, the Hon'ble supreme court has, in Sumeti Vij Vs. Paramount Tech Fab Industries [CrA 292 OF 2021] held that: "The statement of the accused recorded under Section 313 of the Code is not substantive evidence of defence, but only an opportunity to the accused to explain the incriminating circumstances appearing in the prosecution case of the accused." Thus, in a nutshell, the law regarding the presumption for the offence under Section 138 N.I. Act is that rebuttable presumptions under Sections 118(a) and 139 of the act have to be compulsorily raised as soon as execution of cheque by accused is admitted or proved by the complainant and thereafter burden is shifted upon the accused to prove otherwise. To contest this, the defence has relied on the statement of the complainant where he testified in cross examination that typically, storage charges are paid by the shipper (here, the complainant) to the port authorities. As it is conclusively established that the hold was placed at the request of the accused persons and not at the CC NI Act 44830/2019 Digitally signed M/s Muskan Containers Line Pvt. Ltd. Vs. M/s All Bound Global Freight Pvt. Ltd. by ARVIND ARVIND TOMAR Date: TOMAR complainant's own whim, it would be incorrect to burden the complainant with the resulting charges. Therefore, his claim for reimbursement is both reasonable and justified. 18.9 The accused persons further contest the liability to pay, on the ground that they are a mere custom broker house acting as an agent of the original consignor Shree Siddhi Vinayak Export and Import Pvt. Ltd. and if any liability to pay to the complainant exists, it would be of the original consignor and not the accused persons. Ld. Counsel on behalf of the accused persons has submitted that the complainant has no where specified the amount it has allegedly incurred as storage charges to suggest that this cheque was paid in lieu thereof. To cast a shadow of doubt on the case of the complainant, he has relied on the statement given by the complainant during his cross examination where he has stated " the total cost of the detention would be Rs. 50 to 60 lacs. 18.12 The accused has relied on the judgments of the Hon'ble supreme court of India in the cases of M/S Indus Airways Pvt. Ltd and Ors vs M/S Magnum Aviation Pvt Ltd and ors. (AIR ONLINE 2014 SC 89) and Sampelly Satyanarayana Rao v. Indian Renewable Energy Development Agency Limited (AIR 2016 SUPREME COURT 4363) to rebut the case of the complainant. The Hon'ble Supreme court of India in para 13 of Indus Airways judgment has held that "To attract an offence under Section 138, there should be legally enforceable debt or other liability subsisting on the date of drawal of the cheque. In other words, drawal of the cheque in discharge of existing or past adjudicated liability is sine qua non for bringing an offence under Section 138." "The payment by cheque in the nature of advance payment indicates that at the time of drawal of cheque, there was no existing liability." In Sampelly case also, the Hon'ble Supreme Court of India had distinguished between a cheque issued for a debt that had already accrued (existing liability) and one issued for a debt or obligation that would arise in the future (security) and held that liability under S. 138 arises only in cases where the liability is existing.
